lesson.title: Launch angle and range
lesson.objective: Explain how launch angle changes a projectile’s height and landing distance, and identify angles that give the same range.
lesson.approachReason: Changing the launch angle while holding speed fixed lets the learner see the height–distance trade-off before explaining it.

blocks.heading: One speed, two directions
blocks.body:
The **launch angle** is measured upward from the horizontal. At a fixed launch speed, raising the angle gives the projectile more upward speed but less horizontal speed.

More upward speed means a higher peak and more time before returning to launch height. Less horizontal speed means less distance covered each second: the **range**, or horizontal distance to the landing point, depends on both effects.
blocks.example: Your simulated launch at 75° stays in the air longer than the launch at 45°, but lands closer. Extra time cannot fully compensate for its smaller horizontal speed.

hints: Separate motion across the ground from motion upward.
What determines how long the projectile takes to return to its starting height?
blocks.retry: Think of the same launch speed being aimed in a different direction. A steeper launch directs more of that speed upward and less of it horizontally.

blocks.heading: 45° balances the trade-off
blocks.body:
For a fixed launch speed, with no air resistance and landing at launch height, **45° gives the greatest range**. Below 45°, raising the angle increases range; above 45°, raising it decreases range.

In this same model, two angles that add to 90° have equal ranges. They are called **complementary angles**: the steeper launch travels horizontally more slowly, but stays airborne longer, and these effects exactly balance.
blocks.example: The 35° and 55° launches land equally far away because 35° + 55° = 90°. The 55° launch has the higher peak and longer flight. These rules need not hold with air resistance or a different landing height.

hints: First find pairs whose angles add to 90°.
Then compare how close each pair is to the angle that gives maximum range.
blocks.retry: Angles equally far below and above 45° have equal ranges. To compare two such pairs, consider which pair is closer to the maximum-range angle.

blocks.heading: Clear the obstacle, keep the landing point
blocks.prompt:
In an idealized launcher test, a ball launched at 28° lands at a marked spot on level ground. You want a **higher arc that lands at the same spot**, without changing launch speed.

Ignore air resistance. What launch angle should you use?

traps.feedback: Keeping the original angle keeps the range, but does not produce a higher arc.
45° gives maximum range in this model, so it would move the landing point farther away.

hints: You need equal range, not maximum range.
What must the original angle and the new angle add up to?
blocks.solution: The different angle with the same range must add to 90° with the original angle: 90° − 28° = 62°. Because 62° is steeper than 28°, it gives a higher arc while keeping the landing point unchanged.

activities.title: Aim the launcher
activities.prompt: This idealized launcher fires at a fixed speed of 20 m/s, with no air resistance and gravitational acceleration of 9.8 m/s². It lands at the same height it starts. Drag the launch angle to 15°, 45°, and 75°. Compare the peak height and the range—the horizontal position where the curve meets the ground again. Does the highest arc land farthest?
activities.reveal: The 75° launch reaches the highest peak, but the 45° launch lands farthest. Increasing the angle changes height and range in different ways.

bands.title: Higher and farther
bands.detail: Across these settings, raising the angle raises the peak and moves the landing point farther away.

bands.title: Farthest landing
bands.detail: At 45°, the range reaches its maximum for this launch speed and level-ground model.

bands.title: Higher, but closer
bands.detail: Above 45°, raising the angle raises the peak but moves the landing point closer.

activities.title: Compare 35° and 55°
activities.prompt: Using the same idealized launcher, predict how the range at 55° compares with the range at 35°. Both launches have the same speed and land at launch height.
activities.reveal: The ranges are equal, even though the paths differ. Notice that 35° + 55° = 90°: this pairing is the clue.

options.feedback: It stays airborne longer, but its smaller horizontal speed offsets that extra time.
It has greater horizontal speed, but its shorter flight offsets that advantage.
The longer flight at 55° exactly balances its smaller horizontal speed in this model.

questions.question: A student changes a toy launcher’s angle from 20° to 70° while keeping launch speed fixed. Ignore air resistance; the ball lands at launch height. Compared with the 20° launch, how do its initial horizontal speed and total flight time change?
options: Horizontal speed increases; flight time increases.
Horizontal speed decreases; flight time increases.
Horizontal speed stays the same; flight time increases.
Horizontal speed decreases; flight time decreases.
questions.correctAnswer: Horizontal speed decreases; flight time increases.
questions.explanation: A steeper launch directs more of the fixed speed upward and less horizontally. The greater upward speed makes the flight back to launch height last longer.

questions.question: An engineer tests a launcher at 25°, 40°, 50°, and 65°, using the same launch speed each time. With no air resistance and landing at launch height, which two settings tie for the greatest range among these four?
questions.explanation: 40° and 50° add to 90°, so they have equal ranges. They are closer to the maximum-range angle of 45° than the complementary pair 25° and 65°.

trace.blocks: activity > explain > check > activity > explain > check > problem

problems: Hints for the second check and final problem nearly supply the solution procedure, reducing the learner’s opportunity to reason independently.
Check retries mostly restate the original explanations rather than offering genuinely different explanatory approaches.
Two distractors in the second check—40° with 65°, and 25° with 50°—do not clearly represent identifiable misconceptions.
The graph’s angle-dependent bands disclose the range trend during exploration, weakening the intended discovery experience.
